tips.title: A point at the front means OR
tips.body: **AND** is a **D**: flat back, rounded front, no point. **OR** is a **shield** that comes to a **point**. If the shape has a point it is an OR or an XOR — never an AND, however rounded the rest looks.

tips.title: The last operation is the output gate
tips.body: To draw a circuit from an expression, find the operation done **last** — the one joining the main parts — and put it **nearest the output**. Everything in brackets happens first, so it goes **further left**.

tips.title: Read from the inputs, draw from the output
tips.body: Reading a circuit, work **left to right**, naming each gate's output as you reach it. Drawing one, start at the **right** with the last operation. The two tasks run in opposite directions, and using the wrong one is where it goes wrong.

tips.title: NOT takes one input
tips.body: One for NOT, two for AND, OR and XOR. A NOT gate drawn with two wires into it is simply wrong — and it is an easy thing to check before handing the diagram over.

tips.title: Test your circuit with a table
tips.body: A circuit that looks right can still be wired wrongly. Build the truth table and check a row or two against the expression. It takes a minute, and it tests the wiring row by row.

why.matters:
A Boolean expression says what the logic is. A circuit diagram says how it is **built**: inputs on the left, gates wired between them, one output on the right. They are two notations for the same thing, and the specification asks you to go both ways.

Drawing it is not decoration. A circuit makes the order of the operations visible — which gate feeds which — and that order is exactly what an expression hides behind brackets. Getting it wrong is not a drawing mistake; it is a different circuit, doing a different job.

examples.title: Why the same two gates make two different circuits
examples.body:
Take an AND and an OR. Wire the OR first and feed its output into the AND and you get `A AND (B OR C)`. Wire the AND first and feed *its* output into the OR and you get `(A AND B) OR C`. Same gates, same inputs, and the two disagree on **2 of the eight rows**.

With A = 0, B = 0, C = 1 the first gives 0 and the second gives 1. So a question that asks you to draw a circuit is asking about the **wiring**, and the brackets in the expression are the instructions for it.

visual.alt: A truth table of eight rows comparing two circuits built from the same AND and OR gates wired in different orders, which give different outputs on two of the eight rows

examples.title: Why the last operation is the gate nearest the output
examples.body:
Converting an expression into a circuit looks hard until you find the operation that happens **last** — the one joining the main parts. That gate is the one whose output is Q, and everything else feeds into it.

In `(A AND B) OR (NOT C)` the last operation is the OR, so the OR is drawn at the right and the AND and the NOT are drawn behind it. Work backwards from there and the diagram builds itself, in the same order the brackets are resolved.

visual.alt: A logic circuit for A AND B, OR NOT C: the AND gate and the NOT gate sit on the left and both feed the OR gate, which is the last operation and so the one whose output is Q

examples.title: Why a burglar alarm is a circuit you can draw
examples.body:
The rule is: sound the alarm if the system is armed **and** either the door or the window opens. Written down that is `A AND (D OR W)`, and it is three inputs, two gates and a picture a fitter can wire.

Read the table and the behaviour is all there: nothing happens while it is unarmed, however many windows open, and once armed either sensor is enough. That is what a circuit diagram is for — turning a sentence somebody said into something with exactly one meaning.

props.label: A = armed, D = door, W = window

visual.alt: A logic circuit for a burglar alarm: the door and window sensors feed an OR gate whose output goes into an AND gate with the armed switch, with a truth table showing the alarm sounds only when armed and a sensor is triggered

steps.title: The four symbols
steps.body:
A **logic circuit diagram** shows how gates are wired together. Inputs come in on the **left**, wires run between the gates, and the output **Q** leaves on the **right**.

You need four symbols, and they must be drawn distinguishably:

- **NOT** — a **triangle** with a small **circle** on its point. That circle is the part that inverts, and a triangle without it is not a NOT gate.
- **AND** — a **D shape**: flat at the back, a smooth half-circle at the front.
- **OR** — a **shield**: curved at the back, coming to a **point** at the front.
- **XOR** — the OR shield with an **extra curved line** across the back.

The two that get confused are **AND and OR**. The AND is flat at the back and rounded at the front; the OR curves at the back and points at the front. If a shape has a **point**, it is an OR or an XOR, never an AND.

And **XOR is an OR with one extra line**. Leaving that line off turns an XOR into an OR, which changes the circuit's behaviour in one row of its table.

The specification says you will only need **NOT, AND, OR and XOR** within logic circuits — the same four as before, and no others.

steps.title: Wiring matters, not just the gates
steps.body:
Two circuits can use **exactly the same gates** and behave completely differently, because of **how they are wired**. This is worth seeing once, because it is why a circuit must be read carefully rather than recognised at a glance.

Compare:

- $Q = (A + B) . \overline{C}$ — an OR and a NOT feeding an **AND**
- $Q = A + (B . \overline{C})$ — a NOT and an AND feeding an **OR**

Both contain **one OR, one AND and one NOT**. The only difference is which gate is nearest the output. Their truth tables **differ in two of the eight rows**.

So *the circuit has an AND, an OR and a NOT* is not a description of what it does. What it does depends on the **order** — which gate feeds which.

The practical consequence: when a question gives you a circuit, **trace the wires**. Do not simply list the gates you can see and assume the obvious combination.

steps.title: Modifying a circuit
steps.body:
The specification asks you to **create, modify and interpret** circuit diagrams — and *modify* is the one that is easiest to overlook.

A modification question gives you a working circuit and asks for a change: *add an input so the output is also 1 when D is 1*, or *change the circuit so it gives 0 when both A and B are 1*.

The method is to work out **what kind of change the words describe**:

- **Also 1 when…** means another route to an output of 1 — so **OR** the new condition into the existing output.
- **Only when…as well** means an extra requirement — so **AND** the new condition in.
- **Not when…** means the condition must be inverted — so put a **NOT** on it.

Then draw the extra gate **nearest the output**, because it acts on the result of everything before it.

**Check by table.** After modifying, build the truth table and confirm the rows the question mentioned come out right. A modification that looks sensible but changes the wrong rows is an easy mistake, and the table catches it in a minute.

steps.title: Going deeper: the last operation is the output gate
steps.body:
**The single most useful idea.** When converting an expression into a circuit, find the operation that is done **last** — the one joining the main parts — and that gate goes **nearest the output**. Everything else feeds into it.

In $Q = (A + B) . \overline{C}$ the last operation is the **AND**, because the OR and the NOT both have to be worked out before it can act. So the AND is the output gate.

That also tells you how to read brackets: they say **do this first**, which means **draw it further left**.

**Reading a circuit is the same idea backwards.** Start at the inputs, name each gate's output as you reach it, and combine. Working from the output backwards is possible but much harder to keep straight, because you are guessing at what feeds each input.

**Why the same gates can behave differently.** A circuit is not a bag of gates; it is a **structure**. $(A + B) . \overline{C}$ and $A + (B . \overline{C})$ use one OR, one AND and one NOT each, and their tables differ in **two of eight rows**. So an answer that lists the gates has not described the circuit. Trace the wires.

**Make the diagram unambiguous.** A circuit diagram needs more than the right shapes:

- the **correct symbols**, distinguishable from each other
- the **inputs labelled** on the left, the **output labelled Q** on the right
- **wires that clearly connect** — a wire ending near a gate rather than at it can be read as unconnected
- the **right number of inputs to each gate**: NOT takes **one**, the others take **two**

That last one matters. A NOT gate drawn with two inputs is a common slip, and it is simply wrong.

**Check any circuit you draw by building its table** and testing a row or two against the expression. It takes a minute, and it tests the wiring against the expression, row by row.

**And one limit worth knowing.** The specification allows up to **three inputs**, only these four gates, and no NAND or NOR. If a function looks like NAND or NOR, build it from AND or OR followed by NOT.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Inputs go on the **left**, the output **Q** on the **right**.
- **NOT** is a **triangle with a circle** on its point — the circle does the inverting.
- **AND** is a **D shape**: flat back, rounded front, **no point**.
- **OR** is a **shield**: curved back, **pointed** front.
- **XOR** is the OR shield with an **extra curved line** at the back.
- Only **NOT, AND, OR and XOR** appear in circuits on this course, with up to **three inputs**.
- **To read a circuit**: work from the **inputs towards the output**, naming each gate's output as you go.
- **To draw a circuit**: find the **last operation** — that gate goes **nearest the output** — then work out what feeds each input.
- **Brackets mean do this first**, which means **draw it further left**.
- The **same gates wired differently** give different functions: $(A + B) . \overline{C}$ and $A + (B . \overline{C})$ differ in two of eight rows.
- **To modify a circuit**: *also 1 when* means **OR** it in; *only if also* means **AND** it in; *not when* means add a **NOT**.
- Label the inputs and the output, join the wires clearly, and give **NOT one input** and the others **two**.
- **Check a circuit by building its truth table.**

questions.prompt: Describe how to convert the Boolean expression Q = (A + B) . NOT C into a logic circuit diagram, and state what must be labelled.
questions.solution: The first step is to find the operation that is carried out last, because the gate for that operation is the one placed nearest to the output. In this expression the bracketed part A plus B must be worked out first, and the NOT applied to C must also be worked out first, so the last operation is the dot, which represents AND. An AND gate is therefore drawn on the right hand side, and its output is the output of the whole circuit. The first input to that AND gate is A plus B, which is an OR gate with A and B as its two inputs, so an OR gate is drawn to the left and its output is wired into the AND gate. The second input to the AND gate is NOT C, so a NOT gate is drawn, also to the left, with C as its single input, and its output is wired into the AND gate as well. Finally the three inputs A, B and C must be labelled on the far left of the diagram and the output must be labelled Q on the far right. Each wire must be drawn so that it clearly joins the gate it feeds, and the NOT gate must have exactly one input while the AND and OR gates each have two.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Find the last operation.** The bracket $(A + B)$ must be worked out first, and so must $\overline{C}$ — so the **last** operation is the **.**, an **AND**. That gate goes **nearest the output**.

**Build backwards from it.**

- Draw the **AND** gate on the right; its output is **Q**.
- Its first input is $A + B$: an **OR** gate fed by **A** and **B**, drawn to the left, wired into the AND.
- Its second input is $\overline{C}$: a **NOT** gate fed by **C**, also to the left, wired into the AND.

**Label it.** Inputs **A, B and C** on the far left; the output **Q** on the far right.

**And check the details that make it unambiguous:**

- every wire **clearly joins** the gate it feeds
- the **NOT has one input**; the AND and OR have **two** each

A useful final step is to build the truth table and test a row or two against the expression, which checks the wiring.

questions.prompt: Explain why two logic circuits containing exactly the same gates can produce different outputs, using an example.
questions.solution: A logic circuit is not simply a collection of gates but a structure in which the order of the gates, and which gate feeds which, determines what the circuit does. Two circuits can therefore contain exactly the same gates and still behave completely differently. For example, consider a circuit in which A and B feed an OR gate, C feeds a NOT gate, and the outputs of those two gates feed an AND gate, giving the expression A plus B, all ANDed with NOT C. Now consider a second circuit which also contains one OR gate, one AND gate and one NOT gate, but wired so that C feeds the NOT gate, B and the output of the NOT gate feed the AND gate, and A and the output of the AND gate feed the OR gate, giving the expression A OR the quantity B AND NOT C. Both circuits use one OR, one AND and one NOT, but the gate nearest the output is an AND in the first case and an OR in the second. If their truth tables are constructed, they are found to differ in two of the eight rows. For instance when A is one, B is zero and C is one, the first circuit gives zero while the second gives one. This is why a circuit must be read by tracing the wires rather than by listing the gates that appear in it.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The principle.** A circuit is a **structure**, not a bag of gates. Which gate feeds which — and which is nearest the output — decides what it does.

**An example.** Both of these use **one OR, one AND and one NOT**:

- $Q = (A + B) . \overline{C}$ — A and B into an **OR**, C into a **NOT**, both into an **AND**
- $Q = A + (B . \overline{C})$ — C into a **NOT**, that and B into an **AND**, that and A into an **OR**

The difference is which gate is **nearest the output**: an AND in the first, an OR in the second.

**The consequence.** Their truth tables differ in **two of the eight rows**. When $A = 1$, $B = 0$, $C = 1$ the first gives **0** and the second gives **1**.

**So:** *the circuit has an AND, an OR and a NOT* is not a description of what it does. A circuit must be read by **tracing the wires** from the inputs to the output, not by listing the gates that appear in it.

questions.solution: The circuit is Q = (A ⊕ B) . C. Working column **A ⊕ B**: 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0. C is 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1. The AND gives 1 only where both are 1, in rows 011 and 101: **00010100**.

examTechnique.body:
Draw the four symbols so they are clearly different from each other, especially AND against OR.

Put the inputs on the left and label them, and label the output Q on the right.

To read a circuit, work from the inputs towards the output, writing each gate's output as an expression.

To draw a circuit, find the last operation first and place that gate nearest the output.

Give a NOT gate one input and the others two, and make every wire clearly join the gate it feeds.

After drawing, build the truth table and check a row against the expression.

examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer knows that reading and drawing run in opposite directions, and says which it is doing. It finds the last operation before drawing anything, so the output gate is right from the start and the rest follows. It treats a circuit as a structure rather than a set of gates, and can show with a truth table that the same gates wired differently give a different function. It labels inputs and output without being told, checks that a NOT has one input, and verifies the finished circuit against its expression with a table.
